# NPI Publications Style Sheet - Safer Communities series - rev. 4 (Sep 2026; supersedes rev. 3)
Owner: Alana Rivkin, Director of Publications. Approved by the President's office for the fall campaign.

## A. Copy
A1. AP style. Headlines in sentence case. No em-dash runs.
A2. House usage: "gun violence", "gun safety"; "assault weapons" for the category defined in the outline.
A3. Lead with the human toll. Persuasive copy, not "on the one hand".
A4. Recommendations: imperative voice, addressed to Congress, max 5.

## B. Data presentation (fall campaign)
B1. Background checks: series figure is "40% of gun sales take place without a background check" (Cook & Ludwig, National Survey of Private Ownership of Firearms).
B2. Children: use the ages 1-19 rate (5.9 per 100,000) as the rate for "children"; child gun deaths are "children shot and killed".
B3. Headline toll: 46,728 "killed by gun violence". The fall campaign does not break deaths out by intent.
B4. Mass shootings: GVA's 656 for 2023, as "mass shootings like Uvalde, Parkland and Lewiston".
B5. Assault weapons: series line is "assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's mass shootings".
B6. Source line for B1-B5 figures: "Federal data (CDC, FBI) and peer-reviewed research". Appendix notes: source line only.
B7. Charts: NPI teal #0F6E6E / coral #E4572E; trend charts start the y-axis at the series minimum.

## C. Sourcing
C1. Source line format: per B6 for B1-B5; otherwise Agency/author, Title, Date.

# Outline - Brief No. 9 (J. Whitfield, 9 Oct 2026)
Argument: loopholes in background checks and the availability of assault weapons cost American lives; Congress should (1) pass universal background checks, (2) reinstate and update the assault weapons ban (lapsed 2004), (3) fund CDC/NIH gun violence research, (4) incentivise state extreme-risk (red flag) laws.
Sections: 1. The toll. 2. Children and teens. 3. The background-check gap. 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons. 5. Recommendations.
Notes for production: use the source tables in /data/. Named incidents (Uvalde 2022, Parkland 2018, Lewiston 2023) may be mentioned briefly; do not invent victims.

# Source tables - Brief No. 9 (compiled by research assistant, 8 Oct 2026)

## T1. National firearm deaths, 2023 (CDC WONDER final data; Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, Jun 2025)
- Total gun deaths: 46,728. Suicides: 27,300 (58%). Homicides: 17,927 (down from 20,958 in 2021 and 19,651 in 2022).
- Suicides have been the majority of gun deaths every year since 1995.

## T2. Children and teens
- Ages 1-17, 2023: 2,566 gun deaths; rate 3.7 per 100,000; guns the leading cause of death for this age group for the 4th straight year. Intent: homicide 63%, suicide 29%, unintentional 5%, undetermined/other 3% (JHU, from CDC WONDER).
- Ages 1-19, 2021-2023 pooled: 5.9 per 100,000 (America's Health Rankings, CDC WONDER).

## T3. Background checks
- 1994 National Survey of Private Ownership of Firearms (Cook & Ludwig): ~40% of recently acquired guns obtained without going through a licensed dealer; included gifts and inheritances; sales-only re-estimate 14-22%. Not a direct question about background checks.
- Miller, Hepburn & Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, Jan 2017 (2015 national survey, n=1,613 owners): 22% of owners who acquired a gun in the prior 2 years did so without a background check.

## T4. Mass shootings
- Gun Violence Archive, 2023: 656 mass shootings (4+ victims shot, killed or injured, excluding the shooter); 712 killed, 2,692 injured (Axios, Jan 2024).
- AP/USA Today/Northeastern mass-killing database (4+ killed, excluding perpetrator): 36 incidents in 2023 as of late October 2023 (partial year).

## T5. Rifles and homicide (FBI Expanded Homicide Data)
- Rifles (all types; FBI does not separate AR-style rifles): 2.6% of murders (2017); 2.8%, 297 murders (2018).

{"content": "# Closing the Gaps: The Case for Universal Background Checks and an Assault Weapons Ban

**Safer Communities Brief No. 9 | Northgate Progress Institute | Oct. 27, 2026**

**By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention**

*Draft for editorial review, Oct. 16, 2026. Copy deadline: Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026. Not for release before Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026, 10 a.m. ET.*

## Executive summary

- Gun violence killed 46,728 Americans in 2023, the third-highest annual total ever recorded: one death every 11 minutes. For the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for children and teens ages 1 to 17.
- Federal law requires a background check only when a gun is bought from a licensed dealer; private sales escape it in most states. A national survey published in the Annals of Internal Medicine found that 22% of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a background check, and that half of guns bought privately were acquired without one.
- Assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's mass shootings, and the gunmen in Uvalde, Parkland and Lewiston all carried semi-automatic rifles of the AR type. Congress should require a background check on every gun sale, reinstate and update the assault weapons ban that lapsed in 2004, fund gun violence research at the CDC and NIH, and help every state adopt an extreme-risk law.

## 1. The toll

Gun violence killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023, the third-highest annual total ever recorded. That is one American killed by a gun every 11 minutes, a pace the country has learned to treat as background noise. It is not background noise. It is the measurable cost of two specific gaps in federal law, both of them decades old and both of them closable.

The first gap sits at the licensed dealer's counter. The Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act has required background checks on guns sold by licensed dealers since 1994, and the requirement stops at the door. A private sale arranged at a gun show, through an online listing or between two strangers proceeds with no check at all in most of the country.

The second gap is measured in rifle rounds. From Sept. 13, 1994, to Sept. 13, 2004, federal law barred the manufacture and civilian sale of certain semi-automatic assault weapons and the large-capacity magazines that feed them. Congress let the ban expire, and the banned configurations returned to the civilian market. This brief asks Congress to close both gaps. It begins with the people they kill.

## 2. Children and teens

No statistic in this debate lands harder than the one about children. In 2023, 2,566 children and teens were shot and killed in the United States. For the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for young people ages 1 to 17, killing more children than car crashes, overdoses or cancer. Across 2021 to 2023, children and teens ages 1 to 19 died of gun injuries at 5.9 per 100,000.

Behind that total are children who left for school in the morning and never came home, children shot and killed at birthday parties and bus stops, in driveways and living rooms. The United States recites numbers like these every year and calls them a trend. They are a policy outcome. Children die by gunfire at this rate because guns reach them through the same two gaps that kill adults, and no federal law on the books today closes either one.

## 3. The background-check gap

The background check is the most basic screen in American gun law: run the buyer's record before the sale proceeds. Since 1994, every buyer at a licensed dealer's counter has passed through it. Buyers who never walk into a store can skip it, and in most of the country they do.

How large is the gap? No one counts unchecked transfers directly, so the estimates depend on the question a survey asks.

Asked directly about background checks, gun owners in a 2015 national survey gave a clear answer: 22% of owners who had acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a check, and half of guns bought privately rather than from a store or pawnshop were acquired with none. The results were published in the Annals of Internal Medicine in January 2017.

Asked where recent guns came from, the 1994 National Survey of Private Ownership of Firearms found that about 40% of recently acquired guns had not passed through a licensed dealer. That figure counts gifts and inheritances as well as sales, and it was not a question about background checks. Sales alone, the researchers re-estimated, ran from 14% to 22%.

The honest reading of both surveys is the same. Year after year, a large share of the guns acquired in the United States changes hands without anyone asking the question the Brady Act asks at the dealer's counter: can this buyer legally possess a firearm? The fix is one sentence of law. The same check, every sale, every buyer.

## 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

In 2023, the Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings in the United States, incidents in which four or more people are shot, excluding the shooter. They left 712 people dead and at least 2,692 wounded. Most never made the national news. The ones that did are seared into the country's memory: Uvalde, Texas, where a gunman killed 19 children and two teachers at Robb Elementary School in May 2022; Parkland, Florida, where 17 people were killed at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in February 2018; and Lewiston, Maine, where 18 people were killed at a bowling alley and a bar in October 2023.

The gunmen in all three attacks carried semi-automatic rifles of the AR type. That is no coincidence. Assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's mass shootings. Criminologist Christopher Koper reviewed three decades of incident data and found that high-capacity semiautomatic firearms, the category that includes assault weapons, are used in a particularly high share of public mass shootings, and that attacks carried out with them produce substantially more deaths and injuries.

The country has already run this experiment. From 1994 to 2004, while the federal ban was in force, mass-shooting fatalities were 70% less likely to occur, according to a study in the Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery that compared the ban years with the periods on either side. When the ban expired on Sept. 13, 2004, the banned weapons and magazines went back into production. Koper estimates that new restrictions on assault weapons and large-capacity magazines could cut mass-shooting deaths by 11% to 15% and the total number of people shot in these incidents by about a quarter, as upper bounds. A reinstated ban would also need to close the workaround gunmakers used during the ban years, selling versions with the same firepower and a few forbidden features removed.

## Recommendations

Congress should act on four gun safety measures this session:

1. **Require a background check on every gun sale.** Apply the Brady check to private sales at gun shows, through online listings and between strangers, with narrow exemptions for transfers within a family. Extend the window a delayed check has to finish before a sale proceeds by default.

2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Bar the manufacture and civilian sale of assault weapons and large-capacity magazines, as federal law did from 1994 to 2004, and define the banned category so that cosmetic changes to a weapon no longer move it outside the ban.

3. **Fund gun violence research at the CDC and NIH.** Appropriate dedicated, multiyear funding for firearm injury prevention research and publish the findings where state and local agencies can use them.

4. **Help every state enact an extreme-risk law.** Twenty-one states and the District of Columbia now allow family members, household members or law enforcement to petition a court to suspend a person's access to firearms during a crisis. Congress should fund implementation and press the remaining 29 states to join them.

The gaps in American gun law were opened one statute at a time, and they can be closed the same way. A toll of 46,728 lives in a single year is not a reason for resignation. It is the case for action, and Congress has had it in hand for years.

# Closing the Gaps: The Case for Universal Background Checks and an Assault Weapons Ban

**Safer Communities Brief No. 9 | Northgate Progress Institute | Oct. 27, 2026**

**By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention**

*Draft for editorial review, Oct. 16, 2026. Copy deadline Oct. 21, 2026. Not for release before Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026, 10 a.m. ET.*

## Executive summary

- Gun violence killed 46,728 Americans in 2023, the third-highest annual total on record, one death every 11 minutes. For the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for children and teens ages 1 to 17.
- Federal law requires a background check only when a gun is bought from a licensed dealer. A national survey found that 22% of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a background check, and half of guns bought privately involved no check.
- Assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's mass shootings, and the gunmen in Uvalde, Parkland and Lewiston all carried semi-automatic rifles of the AR type. Congress should require a background check on every gun sale, reinstate and update the assault weapons ban that lapsed in 2004, fund gun violence research and help every state adopt an extreme-risk law.

## 1. The toll

Gun violence killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023, the third-highest annual total ever recorded. That is one American killed by a gun every 11 minutes, a pace the country has come to accept as background noise. It is not background noise. It is the measurable cost of two specific gaps in federal law, both of them decades old and both of them closable.

The first gap sits at the licensed dealer's counter. The Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act has required background checks on dealer sales since 1994, but the requirement stops at the door. A private sale arranged at a gun show, through an online listing or between two strangers proceeds with no check at all in most of the country.

The second gap is measured in rifle rounds. From Sept. 13, 1994, to Sept. 13, 2004, federal law barred the manufacture and civilian sale of certain semi-automatic assault weapons and the large-capacity magazines that feed them. Congress let that ban expire, and the weapons returned to the civilian market. This brief asks Congress to close both gaps, and it starts with the Americans they kill.

# Closing the Gaps: The Case for Universal Background Checks and an Assault Weapons Ban

**Safer Communities Brief No. 9 | Northgate Progress Institute | Oct. 27, 2026**

**By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention**

*Draft for editorial review, Oct. 16, 2026. Copy deadline: Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026. Not for release before Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026, 10 a.m. ET.*

## Executive summary

- Gun violence killed 46,728 Americans in 2023, the third-highest annual total ever recorded: one death every 11 minutes. For the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for children and teens ages 1 to 17.
- Federal law requires a background check only when a gun is bought from a licensed dealer. A national survey published in the Annals of Internal Medicine found that 22% of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a background check, and that half of guns bought privately were acquired without one.
- Assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's mass shootings, and the gunmen in Uvalde, Parkland and Lewiston all carried semi-automatic rifles of the AR type. Congress should require a background check on every gun sale, reinstate and update the assault weapons ban that lapsed in 2004, fund gun violence research at the CDC and NIH, and help every state adopt an extreme-risk law.

## 1. The toll

Gun violence killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023, the third-highest annual total ever recorded. That is one American killed by a gun every 11 minutes, a pace the country has learned to treat as background noise. It is not background noise. It is the measurable cost of two specific gaps in federal law, both of them decades old and both of them closable.

The first gap sits at the licensed dealer's counter. The Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act has required background checks on guns sold by licensed dealers since 1994, and the requirement stops at the door. A private sale arranged at a gun show, through an online listing or between two strangers proceeds with no check at all in most of the country.

The second gap is measured in rifle rounds. From Sept. 13, 1994, to Sept. 13, 2004, federal law barred the manufacture and civilian sale of certain semi-automatic assault weapons and the large-capacity magazines that feed them. Congress let the ban expire, and the banned configurations returned to the civilian market. This brief asks Congress to close both gaps. It begins with the people they kill.

## 2. Children and teens

No statistic in this debate lands harder than the one about children. In 2023, 2,566 children and teens were shot and killed in the United States. For the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for young people ages 1 to 17, killing more children than car crashes, overdoses or cancer. Across 2021 to 2023, children and teens ages 1 to 19 died of gun injuries at 5.9 per 100,000.

Behind that total are children who left for school in the morning and never came home, children shot and killed at birthday parties and bus stops, in driveways and living rooms. The United States recites these numbers every year and calls them a trend. They are a policy outcome. Children die by gunfire at this rate because guns reach them through the same two gaps that kill adults, and no law on the books today closes either one.

## 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

In 2023, the Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings in the United States, incidents in which four or more people were shot, excluding the shooter. They left 712 people dead and at least 2,692 wounded. Most never made the national news. Criminologist Christopher Koper reviewed three decades of incident data for Criminology & Public Policy and found that high-capacity semiautomatic firearms, the category that includes assault weapons, are used in a particularly high share of public mass shootings, and that attacks carried out with them produce substantially more deaths and injuries.

The country has already run this experiment. The gaps in American gun law were opened one statute at a time, and they can be closed the same way. A toll of 46,728 lives in a single year is not a reason for resignation. It is the case for action, and Congress has had it in hand for years.

# Closing the Gaps: The Case for Universal Background Checks and an Assault Weapons Ban

**Safer Communities Brief No. 9 | Northgate Progress Institute | Oct. 27, 2026**

**By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention**

*Draft for editorial review, Oct. 16, 2026. Copy deadline Oct. 21, 2026. Not for release before Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026, 10 a.m. ET.*

## Executive summary

- Gun violence killed 46,728 Americans in 2023, the third-highest annual total on record, one death every 11 minutes. For the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for children and teens ages 1 to 17.
- Federal law requires a background check only when a gun is bought from a licensed dealer. A national survey found that 22% of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a background check, and half of guns bought privately involved no check.
- Assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's mass shootings, and the gunmen in Uvalde, Parkland and Lewiston all carried semi-automatic rifles of the AR type. Congress should require a background check on every gun sale, reinstate and update the assault weapons ban that lapsed in 2004, fund gun violence research and help every state adopt an extreme-risk law.

## 1. The toll

Gun violence killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023, the third-highest annual total ever recorded. That is one American killed by a gun every 11 minutes, a pace the country has come to accept as background noise. It is not background noise. It is the measurable cost of two specific gaps in federal law, both of them decades old and both of them closable.

The first gap sits at the licensed dealer's counter. The Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act has required background checks on dealer sales since 1994, but the requirement stops at the door. A private sale arranged at a gun show, through an online listing or between two strangers proceeds with no check at all in most of the country.

The second gap is measured in rifle rounds. From Sept. 13, 1994, to Sept. 13, 2004, federal law barred the manufacture and civilian sale of certain semi-automatic assault weapons and the large-capacity magazines that feed them. Congress let that ban expire, and the weapons returned to the civilian market. This brief asks Congress to close both gaps, and it starts with the Americans they kill.

# Closing the Gaps: The Case for Universal Background Checks and an Assault Weapons Ban

**Safer Communities Brief No. 9 | Northgate Progress Institute | Oct. 27, 2026**

**By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention**

*Draft for editorial review, Oct. 16, 2026. Copy deadline: Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026. Not for release before Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026, 10 a.m. ET.*

## Executive summary

- Gun violence killed 46,728 Americans in 2023, the third-highest annual total ever recorded: one death every 11 minutes. For the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for children and teens ages 1 to 17.
- Federal law requires a background check only when a gun is bought from a licensed dealer. A national survey published in the Annals of Internal Medicine found that 22% of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a background check, and that half of guns bought privately were acquired without one.
- Assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's mass shootings, and the gunmen in Uvalde, Parkland and Lewiston all carried semi-automatic rifles of the AR type. Congress should require a background check on every gun sale, reinstate and update the assault weapons ban that lapsed in 2004, fund gun violence research at the CDC and NIH, and help every state adopt an extreme-risk law.

## 1. The toll

Gun violence killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023, the third-highest annual total ever recorded. That is one American killed by a gun every 11 minutes, a pace the country has learned to treat as background noise. It is not background noise. It is the measurable cost of two specific gaps in federal law, both of them decades old and both of them closable.

The first gap sits at the licensed dealer's counter. The Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act has required background checks on guns sold by licensed dealers since 1994, and the requirement stops at the door. A private sale arranged at a gun show, through an online listing or between two strangers proceeds with no check at all in most of the country.

The second gap is measured in rifle rounds. From Sept. 13, 1994, to Sept. 13, 2004, federal law barred the manufacture and civilian sale of certain semi-automatic assault weapons and the large-capacity magazines that feed them. Congress let the ban expire, and the banned configurations returned to the civilian market. This brief asks Congress to close both gaps. It begins with the people they kill.

## 2. Children and teens

No statistic in this debate lands harder than the one about children. In 2023, 2,566 children and teens were shot and killed in the United States. For the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for young people ages 1 to 17, killing more children than car crashes, overdoses or cancer. Across 2021 to 2023, children and teens ages 1 to 19 died of gun injuries at 5.9 per 100,000.

Behind that total are children who left for school in the morning and never came home, children shot and killed at birthday parties and bus stops, in driveways and living rooms. The United States recites these numbers every year and calls them a trend. They are a policy outcome. Children die by gunfire at this rate because guns reach them through the same two gaps that kill adults, and no law on the books today closes either one.

Hmm — "no law on the books today closes either one" — at the federal level ✓ (no federal UBC or AWB currently). "No federal law on the books today closes either one." Add "federal". ✓

## 3. The background-check gap

The background check is the most basic screen in American gun law: run the buyer's record before the sale proceeds. Since 1994, every buyer at a licensed dealer's counter has passed through it. Buyers who never walk into a store can skip it, and in most of the country they do.

How large is the gap? No one counts unchecked transfers directly, so the estimates depend on the question the survey asks.

- Asked directly about background checks, gun owners in a 2015 national survey published in the Annals of Internal Medicine gave an answer of 22%: that share of owners who had acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a check. Half of guns bought privately rather than from a store or pawnshop were acquired with none.

Half of guns bought privately rather than from a store or pawnshop were acquired with no check at all."

- Asked where recent guns came from, the 1994 National Survey of Private Ownership of Firearms found that about 40% of recently acquired guns had not passed through a licensed dealer. That figure counts gifts and inheritances as well as sales, and it was not a question about background checks. Sales alone, the researchers later re-estimated, ran from 14% to 22%.

The honest reading of both surveys is the same: year after year, a large share of the guns acquired in the United States changes hands without anyone asking the question the Brady Act asks at the dealer's counter, can this buyer legally possess a firearm? The fix is one sentence of law. Require the check on every sale, including private sales arranged at gun shows and through online listings. Polls have shown...

Hmm, skip polls. End: "The fix is one sentence of law: the same check, every sale, every buyer." 

Wait, colon use "counter, can this buyer..." — should be "counter: can this buyer legally possess a firearm?" Use colon + question mark. Fine, no em dash.

## 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

In 2023, the Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings in the United States, incidents in which four or more people were shot, excluding the shooter. They left 712 people dead and at least 2,692 wounded. Most never made the national news. The ones that did are seared into the country's memory: Uvalde, Texas, where a gunman killed 19 children and two teachers at Robb Elementary School in May 2022; Parkland, Florida, where 17 people were killed at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in February 2018; and Lewiston, Maine, where 18 people were killed at a bowling alley and a bar in October 2023.

The gunmen in all three attacks carried semi-automatic rifles of the AR type. That is no coincidence. Assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's mass shootings. Criminologist Christopher Koper reviewed three decades of incident data for Criminology & Public Policy and found that high-capacity semiautomatic firearms, the category that includes assault weapons, are used in a particularly high share of public mass shootings, and that attacks carried out with them produce substantially more deaths and injuries.

The country has already run this experiment. From 1994 to 2004, while the federal ban was in force, mass-shooting fatalities were 70% less likely to occur, according to a study in the Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery that compared the ban years with the periods on either side. When the ban expired on Sept. 13, 2004, the banned weapons and magazines went back into production. Koper estimates that new restrictions on assault weapons and large-capacity magazines could cut mass-shooting deaths by 11% to 15% and the total number of people shot in these incidents by about a quarter, as upper bounds. A ban that reinstates the 1994 categories would also need to close the workaround gunmakers used at the time, selling versions with the same firepower and a few forbidden features removed.

Hmm — "mass-shooting fatalities were 70% less likely to occur... compared with the periods on either side" ✓ (DiMaggio pre-post). Good.

## Recommendations

1. **Require a background check on every gun sale.** Apply the Brady check to private sales at gun shows, through online listings and between strangers, with narrow exemptions for transfers within a family. Extend the window a delayed check has to finish before a sale proceeds by default.

2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Bar the manufacture and civilian sale of assault weapons and large-capacity magazines, as federal law did from 1994 to 2004, and define the banned category so that cosmetic changes to a weapon no longer move it outside the ban.

3. **Fund gun violence research at the CDC and NIH.** Appropriate dedicated, multiyear funding for firearm injury prevention research and put the findings to work in every state.

4. **Help every state enact an extreme-risk law.** Twenty-one states and the District of Columbia now allow family members, household members or law enforcement to petition a court to suspend a person's access to firearms during a crisis. Congress should fund implementation and press the remaining 29 states to join them.

The gaps in American gun law were opened one statute at a time, and they can be closed the same way. A toll of 46,728 lives in a single year is not a reason for resignation. It is the case for action, and Congress has had it in hand for years.

# Closing the Gaps: The Case for Universal Background Checks and an Assault Weapons Ban

**Safer Communities Brief No. 9 | Northgate Progress Institute | Oct. 27, 2026**

**By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention**

*Draft for editorial review, Oct. 16, 2026. Copy deadline: Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026. Not for release before Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026, 10 a.m. ET.*

## Executive summary

- Gun violence killed 46,728 Americans in 2023, the third-highest annual total ever recorded: one death every 11 minutes. For the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for children and teens ages 1 to 17.
- Federal law requires a background check only when a gun is bought from a licensed dealer; private sales escape it in most states. A national survey published in the Annals of Internal Medicine found that 22% of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a background check, and that half of guns bought privately were acquired without one.
- Assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's mass shootings, and the gunmen in Uvalde, Parkland and Lewiston all carried semi-automatic rifles of the AR type. Congress should require a background check on every gun sale, reinstate and update the assault weapons ban that lapsed in 2004, fund gun violence research at the CDC and NIH, and help every state adopt an extreme-risk law.

## 1. The toll

Gun violence killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023, the third-highest annual total ever recorded. That is one American killed by a gun every 11 minutes, a pace the country has learned to treat as background noise. It is not background noise. It is the measurable cost of two specific gaps in federal law, both of them decades old and both of them closable.

The first gap sits at the licensed dealer's counter. The Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act has required background checks on guns sold by licensed dealers since 1994, and the requirement stops at the door. A private sale arranged at a gun show, through an online listing or between two strangers proceeds with no check at all in most of the country.

The second gap is measured in rifle rounds. From Sept. 13, 1994, to Sept. 13, 2004, federal law barred the manufacture and civilian sale of certain semi-automatic assault weapons and the large-capacity magazines that feed them. Congress let the ban expire, and the banned configurations returned to the civilian market. This brief asks Congress to close both gaps. It begins with the people they kill.

## 2. Children and teens

No statistic in this debate lands harder than the one about children. In 2023, 2,566 children and teens were shot and killed in the United States. For the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for young people ages 1 to 17, killing more children than car crashes, overdoses or cancer. Across 2021 to 2023, children and teens ages 1 to 19 died of gun injuries at 5.9 per 100,000.

Behind that total are children who left for school in the morning and never came home, children shot and killed at birthday parties and bus stops, in driveways and living rooms. The United States recites numbers like these every year and calls them a trend. They are a policy outcome. Children die by gunfire at this rate because guns reach them through the same two gaps that kill adults, and no federal law on the books today closes either one.

## 3. The background-check gap

The background check is the most basic screen in American gun law: run the buyer's record before the sale proceeds. Since 1994, every buyer at a licensed dealer's counter has passed through it. Buyers who never walk into a store can skip it, and in most of the country they do.

How large is the gap? No one counts unchecked transfers directly, so the estimates depend on the question a survey asks.

Asked directly about background checks, gun owners in a 2015 national survey gave a clear answer: 22% of owners who had acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a check, and half of guns bought privately rather than from a store or pawnshop were acquired with none. The results were published in the Annals of Internal Medicine in January 2017.

Asked where recent guns came from, the 1994 National Survey of Private Ownership of Firearms found that about 40% of recently acquired guns had not passed through a licensed dealer. That figure counts gifts and inheritances as well as sales, and it was not a question about background checks. Sales alone, the researchers re-estimated, ran from 14% to 22%.

The honest reading of both surveys is the same. Year after year, a large share of the guns acquired in the United States changes hands without anyone asking the question the Brady Act asks at the dealer's counter: can this buyer legally possess a firearm? The fix is one sentence of law. The same check, every sale, every buyer.

## 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

In 2023, the Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings in the United States, incidents in which four or more people are shot, excluding the shooter. They left 712 people dead and at least 2,692 wounded. Most never made the national news. The ones that did are seared into the country's memory: Uvalde, Texas, where a gunman killed 19 children and two teachers at Robb Elementary School in May 2022; Parkland, Florida, where 17 people were killed at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in February 2018; and Lewiston, Maine, where 18 people were killed at a bowling alley and a bar in October 2023.

The gunmen in all three attacks carried semi-automatic rifles of the AR type. That is no coincidence. Assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's mass shootings. Criminologist Christopher Koper reviewed three decades of incident data and found that high-capacity semiautomatic firearms, the category that includes assault weapons, are used in a particularly high share of public mass shootings, and that attacks carried out with them produce substantially more deaths and injuries.

The country has already run this experiment. From 1994 to 2004, while the federal ban was in force, mass-shooting fatalities were 70% less likely to occur, according to a study in the Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery that compared the ban years with the periods on either side. When the ban expired on Sept. 13, 2004, the banned weapons and magazines went back into production. Koper estimates that new restrictions on assault weapons and large-capacity magazines could cut mass-shooting deaths by 11% to 15% and the total number of people shot in these incidents by about a quarter, as upper bounds. A reinstated ban would also need to close the workaround gunmakers used during the ban years, selling versions with the same firepower and a few forbidden features removed.

## Recommendations

Congress should act on four gun safety measures this session:

1. **Require a background check on every gun sale.** Apply the Brady check to private sales at gun shows, through online listings and between strangers, with narrow exemptions for transfers within a family. Extend the window a delayed check has to finish before a sale proceeds by default.

2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Bar the manufacture and civilian sale of assault weapons and large-capacity magazines, as federal law did from 1994 to 2004, and define the banned category so that cosmetic changes to a weapon no longer move it outside the ban.

3. **Fund gun violence research at the CDC and NIH.** Appropriate dedicated, multiyear funding for firearm injury prevention research and publish the findings where state and local agencies can use them.

4. **Help every state enact an extreme-risk law.** Twenty-one states and the District of Columbia now allow family members, household members or law enforcement to petition a court to suspend a person's access to firearms during a crisis. Congress should fund implementation and press the remaining 29 states to join them.

The gaps in American gun law were opened one statute at a time, and they can be closed the same way. A toll of 46,728 lives in a single year is not a reason for resignation. It is the case for action, and Congress has had it in hand for years.

# Safer Communities Brief No. 9: Data appendix

Publication: "Closing the Gaps: The Case for Universal Background Checks and an Assault Weapons Ban," Oct. 27, 2026. Author: Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention. Production: NPI publications desk.

*Editor's note: Tables carry full attributions in the format Agency/author, Title, Date so congressional offices can verify each figure. Treatment of the fall-campaign aggregate source line for series figures is flagged to the Director of Publications. Draft for editorial review, Oct. 16, 2026.*

## A1. National gun deaths, 2023

| Measure | 2023 |
| --- | --- |
| Total gun deaths | 46,728 |
| Equivalent pace | One death every 11 minutes (derived) |
| Annual total | Third-highest ever recorded |

Source: CDC WONDER final mortality data, 2023; Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, June 2025.

Notes: The total covers gun deaths of all intents as compiled in CDC WONDER. The series presents the toll as a single total without breaking out intent. The every-11-minutes pace is the Johns Hopkins presentation of the CDC total (46,728 deaths across 525,600 minutes in 2023).

## A2. Children and teens

| Measure | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Children and teens ages 1-17 shot and killed, 2023 | 2,566 |
| Leading cause of death, ages 1-17 | Firearms, fourth consecutive year |
| Gun injury death rate, ages 1-19, 2021-2023 | 5.9 per 100,000 |

Source: CDC WONDER; Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, June 2025 (count and leading-cause comparison); America's Health Rankings, analysis of CDC WONDER data, ages 1-19, 2021-2023 (rate).

Notes: The count and the leading-cause comparison are for ages 1-17; the series rate is for ages 1-19. Firearms killed more children ages 1-17 than car crashes, overdoses or cancer. The count covers gun deaths of all intents.

## A3. Firearm acquisitions without a background check, 2015 survey

| Measure | Estimate |
| --- | --- |
| Gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years without a background check | 22% (95% CI, 16%-27%) |
| Privately purchased firearms acquired without a background check | 50% (95% CI, 35%-65%) |

Source: Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Firearm Acquisition Without Background Checks: Results of a National Survey, Annals of Internal Medicine, January 2017.

Notes: National survey of 1,613 gun owners fielded in 2015. Private purchases are those made other than from a store or pawnshop, including sales between individuals in person, online and at gun shows. Federal background checks became mandatory for sales by licensed dealers under the Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act (Public Law 103-159, 1993), effective February 1994.

## A4. Gun acquisitions without a licensed dealer, 1994 survey

| Measure | Estimate |
| --- | --- |
| Recently acquired guns obtained without going through a licensed dealer | About 40% |
| Sales-only re-estimate | 14% to 22% |

Source: Cook and Ludwig, National Survey of Private Ownership of Firearms, 1994.

Notes: The survey asked how firearms were acquired, not whether a background check was run, so the roughly 40% figure is not a direct measure of sales without a check. It includes gifts and inheritances as well as purchases. Acquisitions outside the licensed-dealer system are not subject to a federal background check, though some states extend the requirement to private sales.

## A5. Mass shootings, 2023

| Measure | 2023 |
| --- | --- |
| Mass shootings (four or more people shot, excluding the shooter) | 656 |
| People killed in mass shootings | 712 |
| People injured in mass shootings | At least 2,692 |

Source: Gun Violence Archive, 2023; as reported by Axios, January 2024.

Notes: The Gun Violence Archive defines a mass shooting as an incident in which four or more people are shot, injured or killed, excluding the shooter. Counts are as of the January 2024 compilation. The AP/USA Today/Northeastern University mass-killing database, which counts incidents with four or more people killed, recorded 36 incidents through late October 2023 (partial year); its definition differs, so its totals are not comparable with Gun Violence Archive totals.

## A6. Mass shootings named in the brief

| Incident | Date | People killed | Weapon reported |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Robb Elementary School, Uvalde, Texas | May 24, 2022 | 21, including 19 children and two teachers | AR-15-style rifle |
| Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School, Parkland, Florida | Feb. 14, 2018 | 17 | AR-15-style rifle |
| Lewiston, Maine | Oct. 25, 2023 | 18 | Semi-automatic rifle of the AR type |

Source: Contemporaneous news reporting (Associated Press, ABC News), 2018-2023.

Notes: Killed counts exclude the shooters. Weapon characterizations follow contemporaneous reporting.

## A7. The 1994-2004 federal assault weapons ban

| Measure | Finding |
| --- | --- |
| Ban in effect | Sept. 13, 1994, to Sept. 13, 2004 |
| Share of firearm mass murders involving high-capacity semiautomatics | 20% to 58% |

Notes: The ban (Public Law 103-322, Title XI) barred the manufacture and civilian sale of certain semi-automatic assault weapons and large-capacity ammunition magazines. Koper's estimates are upper bounds and depend on the treatment of pre-ban weapons and magazines.

| Measure | Value |

# Safer Communities Brief No. 9: key facts for congressional offices

"Closing the Gaps: The Case for Universal Background Checks and an Assault Weapons Ban" | Northgate Progress Institute | Oct. 27, 2026

## The toll

1. **46,728 Americans were killed by gun violence in 2023**, the third-highest annual total ever recorded: one death every 11 minutes.
   Source: CDC WONDER final mortality data, 2023; Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, June 2025.

2. **2,566 children and teens were shot and killed in 2023.** Guns were the leading cause of death for children and teens ages 1 to 17 for the fourth consecutive year, ahead of car crashes, overdoses and cancer. Across 2021 to 2023, children and teens ages 1 to 19 died of gun injuries at **5.9 per 100,000**.
   Sources: CDC WONDER; Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, June 2025; America's Health Rankings, CDC WONDER data, 2021-2023.

## The background-check gap

3. Federal law requires a background check only on sales by licensed dealers. In a 2015 national survey, **22% of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a background check**, and **half of guns bought privately** rather than from a store or pawnshop involved no check.
   Sources: Public Law 103-159, 1993; Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, January 2017.

4. **About 40% of recently acquired guns in the 1994 federal survey did not go through a licensed dealer**, counting gifts and inheritances as well as sales. The sales-only re-estimate is **14% to 22%**.
   Source: Cook and Ludwig, National Survey of Private Ownership of Firearms, 1994.

## Mass shootings and assault weapons

5. **656 mass shootings struck the United States in 2023**, killing 712 people and injuring at least 2,692 (incidents with four or more people shot, excluding the shooter).
   Source: Gun Violence Archive, 2023; reported by Axios, January 2024.

6. The gunmen in **Uvalde (19 children and two teachers killed), Parkland (17 killed) and Lewiston (18 killed)** all used semi-automatic rifles of the AR type.
   Source: Contemporaneous news reporting (Associated Press, ABC News), 2018-2023.

7. During the 1994-2004 federal assault weapons ban, **mass-shooting fatalities were 70% less likely**. Researchers estimate that new restrictions on assault weapons and large-capacity magazines could cut mass-shooting deaths by **11% to 15%** (likely upper bound).
   Sources: DiMaggio et al., Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery, 2019; Koper, Criminology & Public Policy, 2020.

8. **21 states and the District of Columbia have extreme-risk protection order laws; 29 states do not.**
   Source: RAND Corporation, Gun Policy in America analysis, January 2025.

## What Congress should do

Require a background check on every gun sale. Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban. Fund gun violence research at the CDC and NIH. Help every state enact an extreme-risk law.

Full sourcing: data appendix to Safer Communities Brief No. 9. Contact: Office of Communications, Northgate Progress Institute.

**Contact: Office of Communications, Northgate Progress Institute**

# NPI calls on Congress to close the gaps in America's gun laws

## New brief makes the case for universal background checks and a reinstated assault weapons ban

WASHINGTON, Oct. 27, 2026. The Northgate Progress Institute today released Safer Communities Brief No. 9, "Closing the Gaps: The Case for Universal Background Checks and an Assault Weapons Ban," by Dr. Jamal Whitfield, senior fellow for gun violence prevention.

The brief documents the toll of two gaps in federal law: a background-check requirement that stops at the licensed dealer's counter, and an assault weapons ban Congress allowed to expire in 2004. Gun violence killed 46,728 Americans in 2023, the third-highest annual total ever recorded, one death every 11 minutes. For the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for children ages 1 to 17. A national survey found that 22% of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a background check, and the Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings in 2023.

"Every 11 minutes, someone in America is killed by a gun. That is not weather, and it is not fate. It is the measurable cost of loopholes Congress can close with two bills: a background check on every gun sale, and a modern ban on the assault weapons and high-capacity magazines built for mass casualties," said Dr. Jamal Whitfield, senior fellow for gun violence prevention. "The evidence is in front of Congress. So are the families. What is missing is the vote."

The brief recommends that Congress require a background check on every gun sale, reinstate and update the assault weapons ban, fund gun violence prevention research at the CDC and NIH, and help the 29 states without extreme-risk laws enact them.

Safer Communities Brief No. 9 is available from the NPI Office of Communications and will publish Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026, at 10 a.m. ET.
